title: The clique against him, and the band breaking up in New York
summary: Resentment lasted until New York, though Lindsay and Preston Jackson stayed outside the clique; Collins then booked Armstrong alone abroad and the band returned to Chicago.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: You mentioned that when you joined the band in Detroit, and Louis made you musical director and said, it's your band.
That the guys in the band didn't seem to like that. They resented that. Did that continue as time went by?
It continued until we got to New York. Now, that was just a syndicator of the band, a syndicator representing the band, like --

-- and all of us did in there, and a certain element was there. But, now, you take -- like, Johnny Lindsay wasn't in the clique, Preston Jackson wasn't in it. See, he wasn't in it. Mr. Jackson was part of the instigator of me getting in there. He told Louis about me because -- Randolph here is asking what I'm talking about. He says that my arranging -- teaching his wife scoring, you know, and I guess
it became a kick for me, and Preston Jackson told him, and that rang a bell, you know.
Well, the band broke up in New York. Is that correct? In '31.
Oh, the '31 band, yeah. Because Collins booked -- Collins had the band then. Connie's Inn
Collins, Collins. And he booked Louis single overseas. I don't know whether he booked him in London or whether he booked him in Paris.
I think it was London, that time.
London, yes. And then we had to beat it back, when he came back here, back to Chicago.
